While the prose and sensory details are well-crafted, the story relies on several clichés, both in its characterization and its expressions. 

* **Character and Plot Tropes:** The central dynamic relies on the overused trope of the "estranged, out-of-touch city professional returning to his working-class rural roots." Jonas is a textbook cliché of this archetype: he wears an impractical wool coat and smooth leather shoes in the mud, smells of aftershave and train air-conditioning, flashes a "corporate website smile," drives a shiny rental car (juxtaposed directly against his mother's "rusty Caddy"), and can't stop looking at his smartphone. Furthermore, the plot hints at the very common trope of the adult child arriving unannounced with a thick folder of documents to convince an aging parent to sell their property or retire.
* **Clichéd Expressions:** The story also uses standard German idioms that are linguistic clichés, such as *"Es zieht wie Hechtsuppe"* (used by Jonas to complain about the drafty wind) and *"Keine Menschenseele"* ("not a living soul" in the narrative description).
